newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine posts 1996 GNP growth of 6.8 percent.
newsitem.headline: Philippine posts 1996 GNP growth of 6.8 percent.

text.p: The Philippines on Wednesday said gross national product (GNP) grew 6.8 percent last year, lower than expectations but way above 1995's five percent.

Growth of gross domestic product (GDP), which is GNP less income from abroad, was 5.5 percent in 1996 compared with 4.8 percent in 1995, said Socio-Economic Planning Secretary Cielitio Habito, announcing the figures at a news conference.
He said GNP was within expectations of a 6.5 to 7.5 percent growth rate, fuelled by increases in investments, exports and remittances from overseas workers.

But GNP growth slowed in the fourth quarter of 1996 to 6.2 percent year-on-year after averaging 7.1 percent over the first three quarters. Officials have previously said they had expected the full-year growth to be around 7.1 percent or slightly above.
Also, GDP fell short of its six to 6.8 percent growth target in 1996 due to a slowdown in output of garments and rubber products, Habito said.
But the expansion in economic output resulted in real per capita income of 12,261 pesos, 4.4 percent higher than 1995, he said.

"We do expect the economy to accelerate further in 1997. It is targeted to grow between seven and eight percent in GNP terms," he said. "Inflation is targeted to slow down further to around six to 6.5 percent from the 8.4 percent full-year inflation we had in 1996."
Analysts said the figures reflected the fact that the Philippines was well on its way to a sustained steady growth trend.

"I'm not surprised. These are sustainable growth rates. It's not discouraging," said Emma Pante, an economist with the Far East Bank and Trust Co. The bank had expected GNP growth in 1996 at 7.2 percent and GDP growth at 5.5 percent.
"Our expectations (for 1997) of six percent GDP growth and seven to 7.5 percent GNP growth will be attainable," Pante said.
"I think the fourth quarter (slowdown) was expected. The second and third quarters were growing at a blistering pace," said Jose Mario Cuyegkeng, research head of ING Barings Securities.
"The economy is still strong and will move up to around six percent (GDP growth) in 1997, he said, adding that his GNP growth forecast was seven percent for this year.
The government said bullish growth projections this year were anchored on higher exports and lower inflation.

"The lower inflation forecast is likewise expected to stimulate domestic demand...as well as reduce the cost of doing business and so again making it (the country) more attractive as a potential investment site while also perking up further consumer expenditure," Habito said.
But a few threats remained, he cautioned.

"Political preoccupations can actively get in the way of our economic agenda, as far as economic reforms are concerned," he said, referring to the early political campaigning ahead of the May 1998 presidential elections.
"It will affect investment interest. It's going to be a concern," Cuyegkeng said.
Nevertheless, "the reforms initiated since 1991 and pursued aggressively by the current administration are difficult to reverse," he said.
